reason: Branching can be irregular. One example (irregular stripes) is a different thing, but the others fit.
Wrong part. 'spur' here is the spur of a flower or petal (as in Aquilegia, orchids), not a short shoot. The bearer should be a spur class.
A pollinium (pollinarium) can be straight or bent.
Rostellum lobes can spread or diverge. The bare 'slightly spreading' example has no clear bearer.
A corolla lip can end in a tail-like (caudate) apex. Some examples may really be about the apex, not the lip.
The adaxial surface of a petiole can be pubescent. The examples are correct.
The examples (soboles, tubercles, creeping parts) describe organs of the plant, not the whole plant. Whole-plant shape is not elongated in the intended sense; the organ should be the bearer.
A cupule has a width.
Bark colour can be light or pale ('light coloured', 'claire').
A leaf lamina tip can be blunt.
Prickles are described as retrorse (pointing backwards).
Higher-order inflorescence axes can be branched or forked.
Nectar scales and nectaries can be quadrangular or subquadrangular.
'Readily fragmenting' is a tendency of dry stems, not a shape. Some examples are negated. A rule would need to handle tendency words ('readily') and negation.
The examples give the insertion position of the peristome relative to the mouth. They do not say it is inserted into something. The PATO term is the wrong reading.
A spathe can be hooded, saccate or urceolate (concave).
The margin of a leaf lamina lobe can be erose. The quality is taken from the margin onto the lobe.
A tree crown can be oblong.
Sepals can be cream coloured.
The examples describe the spur of the petal ('petaline spur circinate'). The spur is its own part, so petal is the wrong bearer.
A lamina can be narrow. One example is about wings of the lamina, which is a different part.
Pinnules can be hairy.
A lemma can be lanate or woolly.
A lemma can be bristly.
An indusium can be interrupted or discontinuous.
PATO_0000001 is the generic root 'quality'. The examples are about margins (entire, erose, incised), which have their own terms.
Labellum lobes can be falcate (sickle-shaped).
Ray flowers (ray florets) can be hispid.
An inflorescence can be aromatic or scented. A statement naming a specific scent (carrots, prunes) is a different quality.
A mesocarp can be succulent.
A petal base can be truncate.
Inflorescence bracts (spathelles) can be linear.
Hyaline usually applies to the margin of a calyx lobe, not the whole lobe. A rule would need to tell margin-only from whole-organ statements.
Spores can be subspherical.
Deltoid-lanceolate is a triangular-lanceolate shape, and a leaflet can have it.
'Attached at base' gives where the indusium is attached. 'Attached to' needs a target, which these statements do not give. A rule would need an attachment-site pattern.
Leaflets can be regularly arranged. The pattern describes the arrangement of leaflets.
A spathe can be auriculate. One example mentions a throat margin, which may be another organ.
Anther thecae can be sessile.
A spathe can be tubular.
Inflorescence axis internodes can be glabrous or hairy.
'Disk' in the examples may be the disc of a flower head (Asteraceae), not the floral disc. A discoid floral disc is also nearly circular. A rule would need the family or context to tell them apart.
A perianth tube can be hairy or glabrous, inside or outside.
An ovary can be spotted or dotted. One example ('and spots') has no clear bearer.
A guard cell has a length.
'Few' counts how many elements the pappus has. It is not a quality of one element. The count belongs to the pappus or the counted-parts rule.
The examples are about areoles (cactus), not areole buds. The part is wrong. Equal or unequal size also describes a group.
'Phyllaries few' counts the bracts of the involucre. It is not a quality of a single bract. The counted-parts rule should take it.
A leaf sheath auricle can be undulate.
A leaf sheath auricle has a diameter.
Gemmae can be clavate.
A fruit (such as a loment) can be plicate.
A pedicel can be weak. There are only two statements.
A leaf apex can be retuse.
A bracteole can be sepal-like (sepaloid).
Sporangia can be sessile.
Pseudobulbs can be erect.
A corolla lip can have a cuspidate apex. Some examples may be about the apex.
Pseudobulbs can be subglobose or spheroid.
Ray flowers can be filiform.
